newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightist Le Pen feasts on attacks.
newsitem.headline: French far-rightist Le Pen feasts on attacks.

text.p: Whether his critics attack him head-on or just ignore him, the result tends to be the same; French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen always seems to end up stealing the show.

A fiery debater, expert at turning his opponents' arguments back at them, the feisty 68-year-old former Foreign Legionnaire relishes attacks and basks in the publicity which he believes always benefits his National Front.
When ignored, the skilled orator manages some extreme remark which has media and politicians breaking silence and screaming outrage.
Perplexed media and politicians have used both tactics over the years without managing to stop the anti-immigrant activist elbowing his way to the centre of the political stage.
When foes claimed that Saturday's march by tens of thousands of protesters in Strasbourg marked a watershed in opposition to the Front, he said it only highlighted the Front's rise.

Le Pen has displayed through his career the stubbornness for which his Breton sailor ancestors are famous. After volunteering as a Foreign Legion paratrooper in Indochina, he was elected to parliament in 1956 at the age of 28, only to give up his seat and join the French colonial army in Algeria.
Dogged by allegations that he took part in torture sessions against Algerian guerrillas, his first bid for the presidency in 1974 was a flop with 0.7 percent of the votes.

The Front he founded in 1972 began to flourish in the 1980s; it won 35 seats in the National Assembly in 1986 but lost all its seats in the following polls as France dropped the proportional representation system.

Le Pen won 15 percent of the votes on his third presidential bid in 1995 with a blend of hard-right and populist appeals appeals against political corruption, unemployment, crime and immigrant "invaders".
Since then the Front has won control of its first four cities and hopes to break through the first-past-the-post system election system to gain a foothold in parliament next year.
Le Pen's foes call him fascist, racist, xenophobic, anti-Semitic and a liar.
He calls the political establishment corrupt and inept and says attacks against him are attacks on freedom of expression and the thin edge of an intolerant offensive against democracy.

Le Pen's quips often spark fury, like his recent espousal of racial inequality. He has compared European unity with the AIDS virus spread by "Euro-federasts". Describing Nazi extermination gas chambers as a detail in history landed him in court.
The burly former paratrooper has grown heavier, his neck thicker. As his political weight grows, he seeks to project a dapper, more grandfatherly image.
Videos at party rallies show him surrounded by adoring crowds, kissing babies. To opponents who call him a peril for democracy, he says the danger comes from those who seek to silence him.
His public appearances are a mix of U.S. election campaign meetings and pompous fascist-style rallies.
He emerges from obscurity to walk in total silence to the stage, turning to the audience with his fists clenched above his head as the rousing strains of Verdi choruses whip the crowd into a frenzy.
Pacing up and down the stage as he speaks with a microphone attached to his jacket, he mesmerizes supporters. The most mundane statement draws applause. What he says goes without question.
Surrounded by a personnality cult, Le Pen refuses to discuss a successor. His deputies, Bruno Megret and Bruno Gollnisch, lack his gift for rhetoric and talent for galvanising crowds.
